articles.title: Baked Bites: how Frisco students turned a passion for baking into a force for community change
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM At a Baked Bites pop-up in Frisco, Texas, the transaction looks simple: you place a pre-order, you pick up a homemade cookie. Buried inside that small exchange, though, is something more considered. Every dollar goes to charity, and the students packaging those orders have made that the only condition. […]
The post Baked Bites: how Frisco students turned a passion for baking into a force for community change first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

At a Baked Bites pop-up in Frisco, Texas, the transaction looks simple: you place a pre-order, you pick up a homemade cookie. Buried inside that small exchange, though, is something more considered. Every dollar goes to charity, and the students packaging those orders have made that the only condition.

Since launching, Baked Bites has raised more than $8,000 for charitable causes, primarily through its partnership with Frisco Fastpacs, a nonprofit that delivers weekend meal bags to more than 1,200 food-insecure children across Frisco ISD every Friday of the school year. For many of those kids, the bags are the primary source of food when school is not in session.

Who is behind Baked Bites?

Baked Bites is a student-led nonprofit. The founders, Dyuthi Bushipaga, Aditi Puri, Twinkle Jadhav, and Harika Yerramchet, all grew up in Frisco, in the same school district that Frisco Fastpacs serves. They chose to use what they had- a skill for baking and a willingness to show up- to do something about what they saw.

The model’s simplicity is part of its strategy: homemade baked goods, sold through pre-orders and at community pop-ups, with all proceeds going directly to their charity partner. There is no corporate backing or overhead designed to extract from the mission. Just students, cookies, and a community that keeps buying them.

What $8,000 represents

The founders are clear about what that number means to them: not a fundraising milestone, but hundreds of people who chose to spend a few dollars on a cookie and, in doing so, chose to believe their neighbor’s hunger was worth solving.

There is something instructive about the math of small acts. A single weekend bag from Frisco Fastpacs costs the organization very little to fill. Enough of those small purchases, from enough people who showed up to a pop-up or placed a pre-order, and you have fed a lot of children over a lot of Saturdays.

The successful summer season

This summer was Baked Bites’ biggest season yet. Seven to eight bake sales, pop-ups, and community collaborations, each one a chance to bring new people into the loop and expand what the organization can fund.

Their model is highly replicable, and they have expanded their reach with 15 Baked Bites ambassadors from different schools in Texas and California.

Action beyond sharing baked goods

Looking further ahead, the group hopes to partner with more local schools to connect students with resources and encouragement they might not otherwise encounter. And it’s going further than access to food.

They have already had 18+ partnerships, ranging from giving kids opportunities to learn coding to initiatives that help people step away from screens. The team even launched a second Instagram account to share some positive ‘bites of wisdom’.

It is a modest extension of the same instinct that started with selling their homemade sweets: help the people around you with what you have, and keep going. What a sweet solution.

Pre-order details are available through their Instagram, @bbaked_bites, or on their website for anyone in the Frisco area.

Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary.

articles.title: EU announces plan to restrict social media access for under-15s
articles.summary: Under the plans, only children over 15 would be able to set up their own social media accounts.
articles.content:
The EU has announced plans to restrict social media access for under-15s across its member states, in a bid to increase wellbeing and tackle online safety.

Under the plans, there would be a gradual approach to children using social media which would include banning under 13s from accessing platforms.

Those aged 13 to 15 would only be able to access platforms for an hour per day via "mini accounts" set up through their parent or guardian's social media account.

The European Commission said social media companies would need to prove their platforms were safe by design, while EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the move would "put parents back in the driving seat".

She added the legislation - called the EU Kids Act - would give parents "the tools to help their children navigate a safer world".

"Too many children are being exposed too early to an online world they are not ready to navigate - an environment where bullying can follow you home, where every mistake can be recorded forever," von der Leyen said.

Under the act, only children aged 15 and over would be able to set up their own social media accounts.

But von der Leyen told the EU Parliament on Thursday that "an age limit does not mean letting tech companies off the hook for the content on the platform".

She added that under the legislation - if it is approved - companies would be required to submit detailed child safety plans.

"For every person under 18, the platforms must follow the principal of safety by design, no toxic or addictive features, no traps, etc," she said.

The proposal sets out that age would be verified using the EU's preexisting age verification app.

Von der Leyen had previously proposed a social media "delay" for children in Europe, saying in May that "the discussion about a minimum age for social media can no longer be ignored".

The policy, formally outlined on Thursday, was also trailed in the EU chief's annual address on Wednesday.

Some individual EU countries have already announced their own separate plans to restrict social media for children, including France and Spain.

Any potential EU-wide legislation would supersede those, but it would be possible for individual EU members to then go further than the bloc's action.

It is not clear which platforms the proposed bloc-wide measures would apply to, but von der Leyen said the Commission had "looked at Australia" when putting together the proposal.

Platforms like Instagram, Snapchat and TikTok were banned for under-16s in Australia in December last year.

The ban has been difficult for the country to enforce, with its Communications Minister Anika Wells admitting earlier this month that so far no tech firm had been fined despite research showing many under-16s were still on platforms.

A similar ban for under-16s is set to come into force in the UK in spring next year.
articles.reasoning: The EU's plan to restrict social media access for under-15s aims to protect children's wellbeing and online safety on a broad scale. It introduces meaningful regulations requiring platforms to be safe by design and empowers parents, addressing a significant societal issue with clear policy details and potential large-scale impact.
articles.personality_title: EU plans new rules to protect children under 15 on social media
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The European Union (EU) wants to make social media safer for children. Right now, many kids under 15 can easily create accounts and spend lots of time online, which can sometimes lead to problems like bullying or addiction.

**What happened** – The EU announced a new plan called the EU Kids Act. It would stop children under 13 from using social media at all. Kids aged 13 to 15 could only use special “mini accounts” for one hour a day, controlled by their parents or guardians. Only children 15 and older could create their own accounts. Social media companies would need to prove their platforms are safe and remove harmful or addictive features.

**Impact** – This plan is important because it tries to protect children from online dangers early on. It also gives parents more control over how their kids use social media. The rules would apply across all EU countries, making it easier to keep children safe everywhere in Europe. The law would also require companies to design their platforms with children’s safety in mind.

**What's next step** – The EU Parliament still needs to approve the law. If it passes, social media companies will have to create detailed safety plans and use the EU’s age verification app to check users’ ages. Some countries like France and Spain already have similar rules, and this law would set a common standard while allowing countries to make even stronger rules if they want.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The EU is working to limit social media use for children under 15 to improve safety and give parents more control over their online experience.

Aujourd’hui, de nombreux enfants de moins de 15 ans peuvent facilement créer des comptes et passer beaucoup de temps en ligne, ce qui peut parfois causer des problèmes comme le harcèlement ou l’addiction.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – L’UE a annoncé un nouveau projet appelé la loi EU Kids Act. Il interdirait aux enfants de moins de 13 ans d’utiliser les réseaux sociaux. Les enfants de 13 à 15 ans ne pourraient utiliser que des « mini-comptes » pendant une heure par jour, contrôlés par leurs parents ou tuteurs. Seuls les enfants de 15 ans et plus pourraient créer leur propre compte. Les entreprises de réseaux sociaux devraient prouver que leurs plateformes sont sûres et supprimer les contenus ou fonctions nocives ou addictives.

**Impact** – Ce projet est important car il vise à protéger les enfants des dangers en ligne dès le plus jeune âge. Il donne aussi plus de contrôle aux parents sur l’utilisation des réseaux sociaux par leurs enfants. Ces règles s’appliqueraient dans tous les pays de l’UE, facilitant la protection des enfants partout en Europe. La loi obligerait aussi les entreprises à concevoir leurs plateformes en pensant à la sécurité des enfants.

**Prochaines étapes** – Le Parlement européen doit encore approuver la loi. Si elle est adoptée, les entreprises devront créer des plans de sécurité précis et utiliser l’application de vérification d’âge de l’UE pour contrôler l’âge des utilisateurs. Certains pays comme la France et l’Espagne ont déjà des règles similaires, et cette loi fixerait un standard commun tout en permettant aux pays d’aller plus loin s’ils le souhaitent.

**Une phrase clé** – L’UE travaille à limiter l’usage des réseaux sociaux pour les enfants de moins de 15 ans afin d’améliorer leur sécurité et de donner plus de contrôle aux parents.

articles.title: AI, climate and conflicts top Guterres’s agenda ahead of General Assembly
articles.summary: Ahead of the UN General Assembly’s high-level week, Secretary-General António Guterres said the world had entered “an era of deep uncertainty” and urged governments to embrace international cooperation to address global threats.
articles.content:
Speaking to reporters six days before world leaders gather in New York, Mr. Guterres identified “three existential threats”: runaway artificial intelligence (AI), the climate crisis and deepening inequalities.

He also reiterated calls for a two-State solution in the Middle East and for a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.

Tweet URL

While he acknowledged the need to reform global institutions, including the UN itself, the Secretary-General stressed that the UN’s promises to maintain peace and protect human rights remain the same.

“Updating our structures can never mean abandoning our principles – it must mean applying those principles with even greater determination,” Mr. Guterres said.

Need for peace

Now more than ever, Mr. Guterres called for Member States to uphold the UN Charter, defend international law, protect human rights, invest in sustainable development and push for peace everywhere.

He highlighted the decimation of Gaza and the Russia-Ukraine war as areas of particular concern, urging leaders to work towards “de-escalation, diplomacy and dialogue” to end these conflicts.

“At this crucial moment in the Middle East, de-escalation must be priority one, priority two and priority three,” the Secretary-General said.

All parties to the conflict in the Middle East must respect navigational rights in the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab Straits and must not harm civilians, Mr. Guterres said.

He also called attention to the suffering of the Palestinian people in Gaza and said Israel’s annexation of the West Bank “must stop.”

More than four years after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Mr. Guterres said there is “no end in sight,” calling for an immediate ceasefire as the first step towards a “just, lasting and comprehensive peace.”

The General Assembly is expected to debate both conflicts next week.

Guardrails on AI development

The Secretary-General dedicated nearly half his remarks to what should be done about the rapid advancement of AI technology.

He recognised AI’s “enormous potential” on issues surrounding health, education and climate, but added that the world “cannot afford to ignore concerns” that AI development is progressing faster than human understanding of its risks.

Comparing AI to other issues of international concern Mr. Guterres said governments must protect their citizens from AI’s risks and that “global cooperation is indispensable.”

As fears mount of an AI arms race between the US and China, the Secretary-General acknowledged “geopolitical divides” and said voluntary pauses on AI development will not work if they are isolated – limited to only a few countries.

“The world cannot afford a race to the bottom on AI safety,” he said.

Mr. Guterres pointed to the UN-founded Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, which he said will inform global discussions by providing the best available evidence on AI’s opportunities and risks.

As world leaders prepare to discuss solutions, the Secretary-General called for guardrails that build trust and “make AI safe, transparent and accountable, with human dignity at the centre.”

“International cooperation is more necessary than ever,” he said.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.title: The long journey from ‘Indigenous’ to citizen in Mozambique
articles.summary: The word Indigenous today belongs, above all, to history. “Mozambican” is the word that was born of the new sovereignty. But understanding the meaning of this citizenship requires remembering the journey that came before.
articles.content:
Under the Portuguese Empire (roughly 1505 until 1975), the word “Indigenous” was not just a descriptive word for the African population of Mozambique. It was a legal category that determined rights, duties, and life possibilities. For Africans in Mozambique — including communities such as the Ronga, Changan, and others in the region — the colonial experience was characterized by deep inequality before the state. Being African and born in Mozambique did not entail being treated as a citizen with the same rights as a European.

A hierarchized citizenship

The Portuguese colonial system established a distinction between the “Indigenous,” “assimilated,” and Portuguese citizens. Most of the African population remained in the category “Indigenous.” Access to formal education, qualified employment, public administration, and other opportunities was much more limited. The education system particularly revealed this inequality.

While the children of colonialists had easier access to the formal school system, African populations faced a differentiated educational system that largely prepared them for subordinate positions in the colonial economy. School was not just a place of learning. It was also an instrument of social organization.

Work, taxes, and mobility

In the countryside, the life of Indigenous people was shaped by taxes, labor obligations, and the needs of the colonial economy. In southern Mozambique, this hierarchical reality was influenced by its proximity to South Africa.

Over decades, thousands of men crossed the border to work in South African mines. Income sent back to their families became an important part of the local economy for many communities. Labor migration was, as such, not just an individual choice. It was part of a regional economic system in which work supported both Mozambican families and South Africa’s mining economy.

Land and authority

Colonial inequality was also evident in people’s relationship with the land. African communities had their own forms of land organization and use, but these forms of ownership and authority were subordinated to the colonial power.

The colonial state could define territories, recognize or replace local authorities, and reorganize land use according to the interests of the colonial administration and economy. As such, colonialism did not just control people. It also controlled the space where people lived and worked.

1961: the end of the category “Indigenous” on paper

In 1961, Portugal formally abolished Indigenous status. It was an important legal change. The formal distinction between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples was ended, and the residents of the colonies were considered Portuguese citizens. But legal equality did not immediately produce social equality.

Decades of exclusion from education, economic inequality, and discrimination would not disappear simply because a law changed. For many Africans, their day-to-day experience continued to be marked by profound inequalities in power and opportunities. The word Indigenous disappeared from official documents, but the social structures built around it remained.

1975: transformed into citizens of an independent country

Real change came with Mozambique's independence on 25 June 1975. For the first time, the African population was no longer legally subordinate to a colonial state and became the political majority of a sovereign state. The new Nationality Law sought to establish who was Mozambican and to create a national community based on citizenship, not colonial categories.

For those who were until then “Indigenous,” this was an important change. A person who had been classified by the colonial state as Indigenous then became recognized as Mozambican. It was not just a name change. It was a change of sovereignty.

Political freedom did not eliminate inequality

Independence did not erase the economic and social consequences of colonialism. Mozambique inherited a mostly rural population, with low levels of schooling and a huge lack of technical workers. The new state was also left with an economy deeply dependent on structures inherited from the colonial period.

As such, those who were previously “Indigenous” gained a new legal and political status, but continued to live, in many cases, in very difficult material conditions. Citizenship was achieved, but not economic equality.

From “Indigenous” to Mozambicans

The history of the Indigenous people of Mozambique can be seen as a long journey, through three key phases. First, the colonial subordination of the African majority, who were governed through a legal category that limited their rights. Then, formal equality came in 1961, which abolished the status of “Indigenous,” but did not remove the inherited social structures. Finally, independence in 1975, when the people became politically sovereign in their own country.

One question remains, though. While independence transformed Indigenous people into citizens equal before the law, to what extent were the inequalities created under the empire actually undone? This question remains relevant because many of the differences in access to education, wealth, land, and opportunities did not appear after independence. They have much older roots.

Citizenship as an achievement

The history of Indigenous people should not be told only as a story of colonial suffering. It is also a story of resistance, adaptation, and transformation. African communities preserved languages, cultures, forms of family organization, religious practices, and systems of solidarity despite colonial attempts to reorganize society. And when independence came, it was these same peoples that constituted the core of Mozambique’s new citizenry.

The word Indigenous today belongs, above all, to history. “Mozambican” is the word that was born of the new sovereignty. But understanding the meaning of this citizenship requires remembering the journey that came before: The time when the majority of Mozambique’s inhabitants lived on their own land without having the same rights as those who ruled the territory. Independence did not create the history of Mozambicans, but it finally gave them a state of their own.

articles.personality_title: Mozambique’s journey from colonial labels to full citizenship
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For many years, people in Mozambique were called “Indigenous” under Portuguese colonial rule. This label was more than a name; it decided who had rights and who didn’t. Africans living there were treated differently from Europeans, with fewer opportunities and less freedom.

**What happened** – In 1961, Portugal ended the official use of the word “Indigenous,” making all colonial residents Portuguese citizens on paper. But true equality was missing. It wasn’t until Mozambique gained independence in 1975 that African Mozambicans became full citizens of their own country, with political freedom and legal recognition.

**Impact** – This change marked an important shift from being controlled and limited by colonial laws to becoming recognized members of a sovereign nation. It showed how a group once denied equal rights gained political power and a national identity. However, many social and economic challenges from the colonial era remained, like limited education and poverty.

**What's next step** – Mozambique continues working to overcome the effects of colonial inequality. Efforts to improve education, economic opportunities, and land rights are key to making citizenship meaningful for everyone. Understanding this history helps guide future progress toward a fairer society.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Mozambique’s move from being labeled “Indigenous” under colonial rule to full citizenship after independence shows how legal freedom is a vital step toward equality, even as work continues to address lasting challenges.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le parcours du Mozambique de l’étiquette coloniale à la pleine citoyenneté
articles.personality_presentation_fr:

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En 1961, le Portugal a supprimé officiellement le statut « Indigène », faisant de tous les résidents coloniaux des citoyens portugais sur le papier. Mais l’égalité réelle manquait. Ce n’est qu’à l’indépendance du Mozambique en 1975 que les Mozambicains africains sont devenus de vrais citoyens de leur propre pays, avec liberté politique et reconnaissance légale.

**Impact** – Ce changement a marqué un tournant important, passant du contrôle colonial à la reconnaissance au sein d’une nation souveraine. Cela montre comment un groupe autrefois privé de droits égaux a gagné du pouvoir politique et une identité nationale. Cependant, de nombreux défis sociaux et économiques hérités de la colonisation subsistaient, comme l’éducation limitée et la pauvreté.

Améliorer l’éducation, les opportunités économiques et les droits fonciers est essentiel pour rendre la citoyenneté réelle pour tous. Comprendre cette histoire aide à guider les progrès vers une société plus juste.

articles.personality_title_es: El camino de Mozambique desde la etiqueta colonial hasta la plena ciudadanía
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante mucho tiempo, las personas en Mozambique fueron llamadas “Indígenas” bajo el dominio colonial portugués. Esta palabra no era solo un nombre; decidía quién tenía derechos y quién no. Los africanos tenían menos oportunidades y libertades que los europeos.

**Qué pasó** – En 1961, Portugal eliminó oficialmente el uso del término “Indígena”, haciendo que todos los residentes coloniales fueran ciudadanos portugueses en papel. Pero la igualdad real no llegó entonces. Fue hasta la independencia de Mozambique en 1975 que los mozambiqueños africanos se convirtieron en ciudadanos plenos de su propio país, con libertad política y reconocimiento legal.

**Impacto** – Este cambio representó una gran transformación, pasando de estar controlados por leyes coloniales a ser reconocidos como miembros de una nación soberana. Muestra cómo un grupo antes privado de derechos iguales ganó poder político e identidad nacional. Sin embargo, muchos desafíos sociales y económicos heredados del colonialismo continuaron, como la educación limitada y la pobreza.

**Próximo paso** – Mozambique sigue trabajando para superar los efectos de la desigualdad colonial. Mejorar la educación, las oportunidades económicas y los derechos sobre la tierra son claves para que la ciudadanía sea real para todos. Entender esta historia ayuda a avanzar hacia una sociedad más justa.

**Mensaje en una frase** – El paso de Mozambique de ser llamado “Indígena” bajo el colonialismo a obtener la plena ciudadanía tras la independencia muestra que la libertad legal es un paso vital hacia la igualdad, aunque los desafíos continúan.
